{
  "hypothesis": "Predicted that limited time horizons at work would increase the preference for helping colleagues over future-oriented work activities, and that this condition would eliminate age-related differences in these preferences.",
  "design": "mixed, with age as a continuous predictor and time horizon condition (unspecified, expanded, limited) as a between-subjects factor.",
  "manipulation_or_predictor": "Experimental manipulation of occupational time horizons via written prompts: 'unspecified' (imagining unscheduled time), 'expanded' (imagining staying with the company considerably longer), and 'limited' (imagining a contract expiring in a few months with a new job offer).",
  "outcome_measure": "Forced-choice preference among three work activities: 'Help a colleague or a friend with a company project' (emotionally meaningful), 'Work on a project that may help you advance your career' (future-oriented), or 'Work on a project that may lead the company in a new direction' (future-oriented).",
  "population_and_setting": "Employed adults recruited via KnowledgePanel of GfK Research in the United States.",
  "sample_size_total": 555,
  "recruitment_and_incentive": "Recruited from a larger study about decisions and regret; no specific incentive for this task mentioned.",
  "analysis_plan": "Logistic regression to test the effect of age and time horizon condition on the likelihood of choosing to help a colleague over future-oriented options, including Age x Condition interaction terms and control variables (FTP, education, personality).",
  "preregistered_or_confirmatory": "not stated",
  "other_methods_notes": "The study used an adapted version of the social partner paradigm. The two future-oriented options were collapsed for the primary analysis. A validation survey with an independent sample was conducted to confirm the effectiveness of the time horizon manipulations and the categorization of the work activities."
}
